headline: The Point Holds Its Breath: Bass Go Dark, Albies Sit on the Threshold
subhead: Water at the Lighthouse is sitting right on the number that starts the fall run early — but nobody's iron has found it yet.
body_markdown:
There's a specific feeling that settles over the Point in the last week of July, and if you've fished this rock long enough you learn to recognize it. The bass have gone quiet in the daylight. The bait's staging instead of running. And everybody who's serious about this game starts checking the water like it owes them money, because somewhere out past Turtle Cove or off the Lighthouse, the first albie of the year is going to show up, and nobody wants to be the guy who missed the first day.

We're not there yet. I'll say that plainly, because I said last week this was the window to watch, and I stand by it — the water off the Point has been sitting right at 69 degrees, which is exactly the number that's historically kicked off the scout schools of false albacore and the first bonito push. But sitting at the threshold and crossing it are two different things, and as of this week I haven't had a confirmed report of either fish, not at the Point rip, not at the Elbow, not at Shagwong. What I have seen is nervous water and a few unexplained boils off Camp Hero that could've been albies, could've been blues working peanut bunker, and I'm not going to tell you it was one or the other just because I want it to be. Keep glass on the horizon this week. The moon's building toward full in early August, and that current strength is exactly what stacks bait against the rips and finally tips this thing over. If I had to bet, I'd say we're inside a week, not two.

While we wait on that, the bread-and-butter fishery at the Point hasn't skipped a beat, it's just moved its hours. With surface temps sitting where they are, the striped bass have gone almost entirely nocturnal. Daytime, they're holding deep on the boulder field structure off North Bar and along the current seams east of the Lighthouse, and they're not interested in much. After dark is when this fishery earns its reputation. I've had my best nights working the incoming tide through the boulder field, working a 9-inch black eel slow along bottom, letting the current do the work instead of ripping it back. The takes come subtle at first — a little extra weight, then the rod loads up — and the fish have been mixed slot-to-overslot class, with a few pushing into the 30s reported out of the surf crowd working North Bar on bunker chunks fished on fish-finder rigs with 6 ounces of lead to hold bottom against that rip current. If you're fishing after dark, fish the last two hours of the incoming into the top of the tide — that's when the current's pushing bait up onto the structure and the bigger fish commit.

Bluefish have been the daytime show, and a good one. Bunker schools are still thick off the south side and around the Point itself, and when the blues get under them it's the kind of surface chaos you can see from the Lighthouse parking lot — diving gulls, popping water, the whole show. These aren't snapper blues either — 8 to 12 pounds has been common, some bigger, and they're murdering everything from bunker spoons to topwater poppers worked fast across the melee. If you find the birds, get there quick, because these blitzes have been short-lived, twenty minutes and gone, the school pushing off with the tide.

Fluke have softened up some in the traditional drift zones as the shallow water's warmed, which tracks with what's happening everywhere else on the Island this time of year — the fish are sliding toward deeper, moving water. Best results have come off the Elbow and along the deeper edges of Frisbee Rock, drifting white Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails in 25 to 35 feet, tipped with a squid strip. It's not been a bent-rod fishery, but a few keepers to 6 pounds have come out of there each trip, and the quality's been decent even where the quantity hasn't.

Porgies remain the honest fishery out here right now — Shagwong Reef and the structure off Cartwright Shoal have been holding good numbers on clam and squid baits fished on standard high-low rigs, and that's a fishery that doesn't care what the water temperature's doing upstairs. If you want a guaranteed bend in the rod with the kids, that's your play this week while the rest of us stare at the horizon waiting for something with a sickle tail to show up.

Looking ahead, I think the next 72 hours are the ones that matter most for the season. The current's building into the full moon, the water's already crossed the line it needs to cross, and historically that combination is what turns "maybe" into "confirmed" out here. My money says the first real albie report comes off the Point rip on a falling tide, likely worked with small epoxy jigs or a Deadly Dick cast into nervous water. Until then, fish the bass at night, chase the blues when the birds tell you to, and keep a rod rigged light just in case the water tips over while you're out there.
